tldr: DeepSeek-R1 shows that pure reinforcement learning — with no supervised fine-tuning warm-up — can induce emergent long-chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs, and that the resulting reasoning patterns can be efficiently distilled into small open-source models.
overview: The paper presents two models: DeepSeek-R1-Zero, trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) directly on a base model using only rule-based accuracy and format rewards, and DeepSeek-R1, which adds a cold-start supervised fine-tuning stage plus two RL stages to fix readability and language-mixing issues. R1-Zero demonstrates that sophisticated reasoning behaviors — self-reflection, verification, and strategy revision — emerge spontaneously from outcome-based RL without any human-labeled reasoning traces. DeepSeek-R1 matches OpenAI o1-1217 on math and coding benchmarks (AIME 2024: 79.8%, MATH-500: 97.3%, Codeforces: 96.3rd percentile) and ranks first on ChatbotArena style-control as of January 2025. A distillation study fine-tunes Qwen and LLaMA base models on 800k samples generated by DeepSeek-R1, yielding models as small as 1.5B parameters that outperform much larger non-reasoning baselines; distillation is shown to be more compute-efficient than applying large-scale RL from scratch to small models.

sections.title: Abstract & 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates replacing SFT-based reasoning pipelines with pure RL, introduces DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1, and sketches the key claim: reasoning behaviors such as reflection and verification emerge organically from outcome-based incentives rather than imitation.

sections.title: 2. DeepSeek-R1-Zero
sections.summary: Describes training DeepSeek-V3-Base with GRPO using only rule-based rewards (accuracy + format); covers the GRPO objective (group-normalized advantage, no value model), the two reward types, the simple prompt template with <think>/<answer> tags, and the observed self-evolution — rising response length, reflective 'wait' moments, and AIME accuracy jumping from 15.6% to 77.9% (86.7% with self-consistency).

sections.title: 2.1 Group Relative Policy Optimization
sections.summary: Derives the GRPO loss: sample G outputs per question, compute advantage as z-scored group reward, clip the importance ratio, and penalize KL divergence from a reference policy — eliminating the separate value model required by PPO and substantially reducing memory and compute overhead.

sections.title: 2.2 Reward Design
sections.summary: Accuracy rewards use deterministic rule-based verifiers (answer matching for math, compiler test cases for code); format rewards enforce <think>…</think> tagging. Neural reward models are deliberately avoided to prevent reward hacking.

sections.title: 2.3 Incentivizing Reasoning & Emergent Behaviors
sections.summary: Documents the self-evolution of DeepSeek-R1-Zero: average response length grows steadily throughout training (driven purely by intrinsic adaptation), reflective language ('wait', 'verify', 'retry') increases 5-7x, and an 'aha moment' appears where the model begins mid-response rethinking — all without being explicitly taught to do so.

sections.title: 3. DeepSeek-R1
sections.summary: Introduces the four-stage pipeline to fix R1-Zero's readability and language-mixing issues: (1) cold-start SFT on thousands of human-aligned long-CoT examples; (2) first RL stage with rule-based + language-consistency rewards; (3) rejection-sampling SFT on ~800k reasoning and non-reasoning trajectories; (4) second RL stage adding a helpfulness/harmlessness reward model over diverse prompts.

sections.title: 3.1 Model-based Rewards
sections.summary: For general (non-reasoning) queries, a helpfulness reward model is trained on 66k preference pairs and a safety reward model on 106k annotated responses; these supplement rule-based rewards in the second RL stage to align the model with human preferences without sacrificing reasoning performance.

sections.title: 3.2 Training Details
sections.summary: First RL stage: GRPO with language-consistency reward, 16 samples per question, 32k-token max length, 400-step reference-model refresh cadence. Second RL stage: 1,700 steps at temperature 0.7, with preference-based rewards applied only in the final 400 steps to limit reward hacking. Total training cost: ~$294k at H800 rental prices.

sections.title: 4. Experiment
sections.summary: Evaluates DeepSeek-R1 and intermediate checkpoints (R1-Dev1–3) across English, code, math, and Chinese benchmarks against Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, and OpenAI o1; ablates the contribution of each pipeline stage, showing each stage adds meaningful gains on its target capability cluster.

sections.title: 5. Ethics and Safety Statement
sections.summary: Acknowledges jailbreak risks inherent to a powerful open-source reasoning model and recommends deployers pair it with an external risk-control layer; notes safety performance is broadly comparable to GPT-4o (2024-05-13) on standard benchmarks.

sections.title: 6. Conclusion, Limitation, and Future Work
sections.summary: Summarises that pure RL can unlock reasoning without large annotation budgets; lists current limits — suboptimal structured output, language mixing in non-Chinese/English queries, sensitivity to few-shot prompting, limited software-engineering RL coverage, and the open problem of reward hacking when reliable verifiers do not exist.

sections.title: Appendix A. Background (DeepSeek-V3 & GRPO vs PPO)
sections.summary: Profiles DeepSeek-V3-Base (671B MoE, 37B active, 14.8T-token pretraining) as the starting point, explains why GRPO is preferred over PPO (no value model, better memory efficiency, more stable KL handling), and shows GRPO outperforms PPO on MATH with less hyperparameter sensitivity.

sections.title: Appendix B. Training Details (Infrastructure, Data Recipe, Hyperparameters)
sections.summary: Describes the four-module RL framework (rollout via vLLM, inference, rule-based reward, training); details the 800k SFT dataset (395k math, 211k code, 10k STEM, 10k logic, 178k general); provides distillation hyperparameters for six released small models (Qwen 1.5B–32B, LLaMA 8B–70B); and documents reward-hacking observations that motivated limiting preference-reward RL steps.

sections.title: Appendix C. Self-Evolution of DeepSeek-R1-Zero
sections.summary: Quantitative analysis of training dynamics: per-difficulty MATH accuracy curves show hard problems (levels 4-5) improving most dramatically; reflective-word frequency rises 5-7x; 'wait'-word usage spikes sharply after step 8000, marking a phase transition in reasoning strategy.

sections.title: Appendix D. Evaluation of DeepSeek-R1
sections.summary: Full benchmark setup (decontamination procedure, zero-shot prompting rationale, pass@k evaluation protocol), main results table against o1-1217 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet, safety evaluation across six public benchmarks and an in-house 28-subcategory taxonomy, multilingual safety across 50 languages, and jailbreak robustness study — DeepSeek-R1 with risk control reaches safety parity with frontier closed-source models.

sections.title: Appendix E. More Analysis
sections.summary: Compares R1 vs V3 performance breakdown by MMLU/MMLU-Pro subject category (R1 gains are largest in STEM); shows R1 generalizes to AIME 2025 (75% solve rate) and achieves a USAMO-qualifying score on AMC 12 2024; analyses adaptive CoT length (difficult problems use 2x+ more thinking tokens); and demonstrates that non-reasoning models cannot close the gap via majority voting alone.

sections.title: Appendix F. DeepSeek-R1 Distillation
sections.summary: Fine-tunes six open-source models (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B through LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct) on the 800k teacher-generated dataset using SFT only; the 1.5B distilled model already beats GPT-4o-0513 on math benchmarks; distillation consistently outperforms applying the same large-scale RL directly to small architectures, confirming that knowledge transfer from a strong teacher is more efficient than RL from scratch at small scale.

sections.title: Appendix G. Discussion (Key Findings & Unsuccessful Attempts)
sections.summary: Emphasises three lessons: base-model capability must be sufficient for RL to work (7B models failed); reliable verifiers are the limiting factor for pure-RL scope; and SFT and RL are complementary rather than substitutable. Documents failed attempts with Process Reward Models (reward hacking, annotation cost) and MCTS (exponential search space, value-model instability).

sections.title: Appendix H–I. Related Work & Open Release
sections.summary: Situates DeepSeek-R1 within CoT prompting, inference-time compute scaling, and RL-for-reasoning literature; announces MIT-licensed open release of DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1-Zero, and all six distilled models on HuggingFace.

readingFocus: R1-Zero as proof-of-concept for pure-RL reasoning (Phase 10): study sections 2.1–2.3 closely — the GRPO objective, the rule-based reward design, and the emergent self-reflection behaviors are the core mechanism Microlab's own RL-reasoning experiments will need to replicate or adapt.

Cold-start + multi-stage RL pipeline (Phase 11): Section 3 and Appendix B.3.2 explain why a small cold-start SFT dataset is needed before RL to stabilise language and readability, and how the two RL stages are sequenced — critical design decisions for Microlab's training pipeline.

Distillation to small models (Appendix F): Table 15 and the distillation vs RL comparison in F.1 quantify exactly how much of R1's reasoning can be transferred via SFT-only fine-tuning; this is directly actionable for Microlab's smaller-model deployment targets in Phases 10-11.

Reward design and reward hacking (sections 2.2, 3.1, appendices B.5, G.2): the paper's deliberate avoidance of neural reward models, the language-consistency reward for multilingual stability, and the documented reward-hacking failure mode with preference models are all practical guardrails for Microlab's own reward engineering.

GRPO vs PPO (Appendix A.3): the worked comparison — no value model, KL added to loss rather than per-token reward, periodic reference-model refresh — is the justification for choosing GRPO; understand this before implementing the RL training loop.

Test-time compute scaling (Appendix E.4): the adaptive CoT-length finding (hard problems use 2x tokens; majority voting complements but does not replace long CoT) informs how Microlab should evaluate and budget inference compute for reasoning tasks.
